title: Thread caches and magazines
summary: Why a locked shared allocator stops scaling, how Bonwick and Adams' magazines and depot bound shared traffic at 1/M, what the caches cost in memory, and how per-thread and rseq per-CPU caches use the idea today.
outcomes: Explain why a single allocator lock caps throughput at 1/c and how per-CPU magazines remove it from the common path
Trace the magazine algorithm (loaded, previous, depot, slab layer) for a given sequence of allocs and frees
Prove why keeping a previous magazine bounds depot traffic at 1/M and compute depot trips for a workload
Compute the worst-case idle memory held by a CPU layer and explain how M is sized and depot memory reclaimed
Compare per-thread caches with rseq-based per-CPU caches and explain how a restartable sequence stays correct

lessons.title: One lock, many cores: why a shared slab cache stops scaling

blocks.md:
From the slab allocator course you know the shape of an object cache: slabs of equal-size chunks, a freelist of free objects, and `kmem_cache_alloc` / `kmem_cache_free` that just move an object on or off that list. Once a cache is warm those calls are only a handful of instructions.

The catch is the word *a*. There is one freelist per cache, so there is one lock per cache. Bonwick and Adams put it bluntly in their 2001 paper: to allocate an object the allocator must take the lock that protects the cache's slab list, which serializes all allocations.

Serializing a 20-instruction operation sounds harmless. It is not, for two reasons you met in the mutex course:

- **Queueing.** While one CPU holds the lock, every other CPU that wants an object waits. The lock turns N cores into a single-file line.
- **Cache line traffic.** The lock word and the freelist head are written by every CPU, so the cache lines holding them bounce between cores on every call, and each handoff costs far more than the work done under the lock.

blocks.title: Three threads, one allocator lock vs local caches

scenes.caption: Simplified model: each thread does 100 ns of its own work, then a 100 ns malloc that must hold the cache lock. All three reach malloc at 100 ns, but only Thread 0 gets the lock.
The lock is FIFO here, so threads 1 and 2 take turns behind Thread 0. Thread 2 waits 200 ns for a 100 ns operation.
After two rounds each, the shared-lock run ends at 700 ns. The waiting (red) grows with every thread you add, while the useful work per thread stays the same.
Same work, but each thread allocates from its own local stash with no shared lock. Everyone finishes at 400 ns. (Simplified: the local path is also cheaper in reality, which only widens the gap.)

blocks.md: A tiny model makes the ceiling explicit. Let each operation spend $a$ ns outside the lock and $c$ ns holding it. With $N$ threads, throughput can never exceed $1/c$, because the lock admits one holder at a time:

blocks.caption: Operations per ns. With a = 300 ns and c = 100 ns, X saturates at 10 M ops/s once N reaches 4. This ignores contention collapse, which makes reality worse.

blocks.title: Throughput ceiling of a single allocator lock

scenes.caption: With a = 300 and c = 100 the shared lock caps throughput at 10 M/s from 4 threads on. Private state keeps rising linearly.
Shrinking the critical section to 40 ns raises the ceiling to 25 M/s, but it is still a ceiling. Only removing the shared lock from the common path removes it.

blocks.md: Bonwick and Adams measured exactly this on a 333 MHz 16-CPU Sun Starfire. The original slab allocator took 743 ns per alloc/free pair on one CPU. As threads were added its total throughput did not just flatten, it *fell*, due to what they called increasingly pathological lock contention.

scenes.caption: Single-CPU throughput from the reported latencies: 1/743 ns = 1.35 M pairs/s for the original slab allocator.
With 16 threads the paper reports magazines at 340 times the original allocator. Working back from the magazine figure gives about 0.13 M pairs/s: ten times worse than one CPU.
The magazine layer: 356 ns per pair on one CPU (2.81 M/s), and the same 356 ns per CPU at 16 threads, so 16 x 2.81 = 44.9 M pairs/s. Perfect linear scaling.

blocks.md: Why not simply give each CPU its own freelist of objects? Because allocations and frees are not balanced per CPU. A network driver may allocate packet buffers on one CPU and free them on another. The freeing CPU's list grows without bound while the allocating CPU's list is always empty, so it falls through to the locked slab layer on every call. A per-CPU cache needs a cheap, batched way to move objects between CPUs. That is what magazines and the depot provide.

A shared lock caps allocator throughput at $1/c$ no matter how many cores you add. The fix is not a faster lock but keeping the common path on state that only one CPU (or thread) touches, and going to shared state rarely and in batches.

blocks.question: A service spends 50 ns per malloc inside a global allocator lock. Ignoring everything else, what is the most mallocs per second the whole machine can do through that lock?
options: 20 million per second, regardless of core count
20 million per second per core
It depends only on how fast each core runs application code
Unlimited, since a mutex costs nothing when uncontended
blocks.explain: One holder at a time, 50 ns each: $1/(50 \text{ ns}) = 2 \times 10^7$ per second for the whole machine. More cores add waiters, not throughput.

blocks.question: Why did the original slab allocator get *slower* in total when going from 1 to 16 threads, rather than just staying flat?
options: Each thread ran its constructors twice
Contention made each lock handoff more expensive (cache line transfers, waiting, wakeups), so the serialized work itself took longer
The Starfire had only one memory controller
The slab layer disabled interrupts
blocks.explain: A flat ceiling assumes the critical section costs the same under load. Under contention the lock and freelist lines move between CPUs on every acquisition and waiters spin or sleep, so each serialized operation gets slower. The paper calls this increasingly pathological lock contention.

lessons.title: The magazine: a per-CPU stack of object pointers

blocks.md:
Bonwick and Adams' answer is named by analogy with automatic weapons. A **magazine** is an array of M pointers to free objects, plus a count of how many slots hold a valid pointer. Each valid pointer is a **round**. Each CPU has its own loaded magazine, so it can serve up to M allocations before it needs to reload.

The magazine is used as a stack. Allocation pops the top round, free pushes onto the top:

blocks.code:
obj = magazine[--rounds];   /* allocate: pop  */
magazine[rounds++] = obj;   /* free: push     */
blocks.caption: The two operations from section 3.1 of the paper. No shared data is touched.

scenes.caption: The loaded magazine holds 3 rounds: pointers to free objects A, B, C. rounds = 3, so the next pop reads slot 2.
malloc pops C and returns it. rounds = 2. Nothing outside this CPU's own structure was read or written.
free(D) pushes D into slot 2. rounds = 3.
free(C) pushes C. The magazine is now full (rounds = M = 4). The next free cannot be served locally.
LIFO means the next malloc gets C back, the object freed most recently. Its cache lines are likely still in this CPU's cache, a bonus the paper points out.

blocks.md: Why an array of pointers instead of linking free objects together through their own memory, as a classic freelist does? The paper gives two reasons. First, writing a link into a free object would overwrite its **constructed state**: slab caches hand out objects whose locks and invariant fields are already initialized. Second, the same allocator manages resources that are not writable memory at all (such as integer ID ranges), so it cannot assume it may store anything inside an object.

When the loaded magazine is empty on alloc or full on free, the CPU must reload. Falling straight through to the slab layer would put a long run of allocations back on the global lock. So each cache keeps a **depot**: a global stockpile of full magazines and empty magazines, protected by its own lock. A CPU trades an empty magazine for a full one (or the reverse) in a single depot visit. The per-CPU part is the **CPU layer**; the CPU layer plus the depot is the **magazine layer**.

scenes.caption: Each CPU owns its magazines. Allocs and frees that hit them touch no shared state at all.
The depot holds whole magazines, not single objects. Its lock is taken once per M objects at most, not once per object.
CPU 0 mostly allocates: it hands back an empty magazine and loads a full one. CPU 1 mostly frees: it hands back a full one and loads an empty. Objects flow between CPUs M at a time.
Only when the depot has no full magazine does an alloc go to the slab layer, for one object, constructing it on the way up. Only when no empty magazine can be allocated does a free go back down.

blocks.md: Each CPU's magazines are still protected by a lock, but a **per-CPU lock** that is almost never contended. The paper chose this over disabling interrupts because some operations (like resizing magazines) must reach into every CPU's state, because disabling interrupts hurts dispatch latency in a real-time kernel, and because on most processors an uncontended lock was cheaper than changing the interrupt level. The whole hot path is this short:

blocks.title: kmem_cache_alloc hot path (Figure 3.1c)

scenes.caption: Index the cache's per-CPU array with this CPU's id. Each element is padded to its own cache line, so CPUs never false-share it.
Take this CPU's lock. Nobody else wants it, so it is acquired without waiting and its cache line is already local.
Rounds available: pop one. Decrement the count, then read that slot.
Release and return. The common case never touches the depot or slab locks.

blocks.md: Per-CPU does not automatically mean scalable. The paper found that padding and aligning each CPU's structure to its own cache line was critical for linear scaling. Without it, the per-CPU counters of neighbouring CPUs share a line and you are back to cache line ping-pong (false sharing).

blocks.question: Why does a magazine store an array of pointers instead of threading a linked list through the free objects themselves?
options: Arrays are always faster to traverse than linked lists
Writing a link into a free object would destroy its constructed state, and some managed resources are not writable memory
Linked lists cannot be used as stacks
The depot needs to sort the objects by address
blocks.explain: Object caches keep free objects in their constructed state (locks initialized, fields set). A freelist link would clobber part of the object. And the slab and magazine code also manage non-memory resources, where there is nowhere to store a link.

blocks.question: CPU 2 only frees packet buffers; CPU 5 only allocates them. With magazines and a depot, how do buffers get from CPU 2 to CPU 5?
options: Each buffer goes back to the slab layer, then CPU 5 takes it from there
CPU 5 steals single objects from CPU 2's magazine under CPU 2's lock
CPU 2 returns full magazines to the depot and CPU 5 loads them, moving M buffers per depot visit
They cannot: each CPU's objects are private forever
blocks.explain: Whole magazines are the unit of exchange. The freeing CPU fills magazines and swaps them for empties at the depot; the allocating CPU swaps empties for those full ones. The depot lock is taken about once per M objects on each side.

lessons.title: Thrashing at the boundary, and why two magazines bound it at 1/M

blocks.md: With one loaded magazine of M rounds, you might expect at most one depot visit per M operations: after a reload you have M rounds (or M free slots) to spend. That intuition is wrong for an unlucky but realistic pattern.

blocks.prompt: Take M = 4 and a single loaded magazine holding exactly 1 round. The workload loops forever: alloc, alloc, free, free. What fraction of these operations visit the globally locked depot?
blocks.reveal: **Half of them, for any M.** The first alloc takes the last round, leaving the magazine empty. The second alloc must swap at the depot for a full magazine and takes one round (M minus 1 left). The first free fills it back to M. The second free finds it full and must swap at the depot for an empty one. Now it holds 1 round again and the cycle repeats: 2 depot trips per 4 operations. The paper calls this **thrashing at a magazine boundary**, and making M bigger does not help.

blocks.md:
The fix is one more slot per CPU: keep the **previously loaded magazine** too. The full rules (Figure 3.1b of the paper) are almost symmetric:

1. If the loaded magazine can serve the request (not empty for alloc, not full for free), do it.
2. Else, if the previous magazine can (full for alloc, empty for free), swap loaded and previous and retry.
3. Else go to the depot: return previous to the depot, move loaded to previous, load a full (alloc) or empty (free) magazine, retry.
4. If the depot has none: an alloc takes one object from the slab layer and constructs it; a free allocates a new empty magazine, or, failing that, destructs the object and returns it to the slab layer.

blocks.title: Loaded + previous, M = 4, loop of alloc, alloc, free, free

scenes.caption: Start at the boundary: loaded holds 1 round (A), previous is empty.
alloc returns A. Loaded is now empty; previous is empty too.
alloc: neither magazine has a round, so go to the depot once. Previous (empty) goes back, the empty loaded becomes previous, a full magazine P Q R S is loaded and S is popped.
free(A) pushes A. Loaded is full.
free(S): loaded is full but previous is empty, so just swap them. S goes into the now-loaded empty magazine. No depot trip.
alloc pops S. Loaded is empty again, previous is full.
alloc: previous is full, so swap and pop A. We are back to the state right after the depot trip (third scene). The loop now runs forever with zero depot trips.

blocks.md: Why does this bound the worst case? The paper's key observation: you only ever go to the depot to replace an empty with a full or a full with an empty. So right after any depot trip the CPU holds one full and one empty magazine (in some order). From there it can do at least M allocations (drain the full one) or at least M frees (fill the empty one) before needing the depot again. Every depot trip therefore buys at least M local operations:

blocks.tex: \text{CPU-layer miss rate} \;\le\; \frac{1}{M}\quad\text{for any sequence of allocs and frees}
blocks.caption: One depot trip per M transactions in the worst case. Balanced alloc/free pairs do much better than this bound.

blocks.title: Simulated depot trips per operation (4,000 ops)

scenes.caption: One loaded magazine, M = 4, starting with 1 round. Pairs never cross the boundary, but the 2-and-2 loop thrashes at 50%. Long runs pay 1/M = 25%.
Loaded plus previous, same M = 4. The 2-and-2 loop costs one depot trip in 4,000 ops (0.03%). Long runs still pay 1/M: 24.9%, the bound is tight for them.
Loaded plus previous with M = 8. Only the long-run pattern, which really does consume M objects per depot visit, is affected: it halves to 12.4%.

blocks.md: The numbers above come from a direct simulation of the Figure 3.1b rules (a script, not measurements). They show the two separate effects: the previous magazine removes boundary thrashing entirely, and M sets the price of genuinely one-sided runs, where an allocating CPU has to fetch a new batch every M objects no matter what.

Two magazines per CPU, one loaded and one previous, guarantee that after every depot trip the CPU holds one full and one empty magazine. That alone bounds depot traffic at 1/M for any workload. Without the previous magazine, an alloc-alloc-free-free loop can send half of all calls to the depot.

blocks.question: A CPU with loaded-plus-previous magazines (M = 10) runs a burst of 1,000 allocations with no frees, starting with a full loaded magazine and an empty previous one. About how many depot visits does it make?
options: About 1, the previous magazine absorbs the rest
About 100
About 500
About 1,000
blocks.explain: One-sided runs are exactly the case the 1/M bound describes. Each depot trip delivers one full magazine of 10 rounds, so 1,000 allocations need roughly 1,000 / 10 = 100 trips (the first 10 come from the magazine already loaded).

blocks.question: A colleague proposes a single-magazine design with M = 64 instead of two magazines with M = 32, arguing it uses the same memory and has a lower 1/M. What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing, a bigger M always lowers depot traffic
Magazine size must be a power of two smaller than 64
A single magazine can still thrash at its boundary: an alloc-alloc-free-free loop hits the depot on half the calls whatever M is
Two magazines double the number of locks taken per alloc
blocks.explain: The 1/M argument only holds when a depot trip leaves you with one full and one empty magazine. With one magazine, a loop straddling the empty/full boundary pays a depot trip every second operation, independent of M.

lessons.title: Sizing M, filling the depot, and the memory you pay

blocks.md:
A magazine layer has to start empty and come to life, choose M, and avoid hoarding memory. The paper handles each with a small rule.

**Populating.** Full magazines are never allocated explicitly. Frees create empty magazines when the depot has none, and full magazines emerge as frees fill them. An alloc that finds no full magazine just takes a single object from the slab layer. (Allocating full magazines on the alloc path would recurse forever the first time the cache that holds magazines themselves needed a magazine.)

**Construction moves up a layer.** The original slab allocator ran constructors when it created a slab. The paper's extreme example: an 8-byte object whose constructor attaches a 1 KB buffer. With 8 KB pages one slab holds about 1,000 such objects (8192 / 8 = 1,024), so constructing the whole slab pins about 1 MB even if only a few objects are ever used. With magazines, the slab layer keeps raw buffers; a buffer is constructed when it moves up into the magazine layer and destructed when it moves back down.

**Choosing M dynamically.** Bigger M means fewer depot trips but more idle objects. Instead of a magic constant, each cache starts with a small M and watches its depot lock. It acquires the depot lock with a non-blocking *trylock* first; if that fails, it takes the lock normally and bumps a contention counter. When the contention rate crosses a fixed threshold, the cache increases M, up to an enforced maximum. The paper reports this settles after several minutes of load, at depot lock contention of less than once per second, on machines from desktops to 64-CPU Starfires.

blocks.title: Depot contention grows the magazine size

scenes.caption: CPU 3's magazines are exhausted, so it visits the depot. It first tries the lock without blocking.
Under heavier load the trylock fails: another CPU is in the depot. CPU 3 falls back to the blocking lock and records one contention event.
When the contention rate passes the threshold, the cache raises M (never above its maximum). Bigger magazines mean each CPU returns to the depot less often.

blocks.md: **The memory bill.** Every round in a magazine is a free object that nobody else can use. Each CPU can hold two magazines, so in the worst case the CPU layer of one cache pins $2 \cdot M \cdot N_{cpu}$ objects, before counting whatever sits in the depot. For 64 CPUs, M = 15 and 512-byte objects that is 64 x 2 x 15 x 512 bytes = 960 KiB for a single cache. A kernel has hundreds of caches, so this is why M should be as small as scalability allows.

blocks.title: Worst-case idle memory in one cache's CPU layer

y.label: KiB held (2 x M x CPUs x size)

scenes.caption: 64 CPUs, 512-byte objects: the worst case grows linearly in M, 960 KiB at M = 15. This upper bound assumes every CPU sits on two full magazines.
On 16 CPUs the same M costs a quarter as much (240 KiB at M = 15). Idle memory scales with the number of caches, CPUs and M together.

blocks.md: **Reclaiming via the depot working set.** In steady state, allocs and frees roughly balance, so the depot's full-magazine count wanders within a band. The paper treats the size of that band as a working set (after Denning). Its example: if the full list varies between 37 and 47 magazines over a period, the working set is 10 magazines and the other 37 can be reclaimed. The kernel depot tracks this continuously but frees the excess only when memory runs low; the user-level port, libumem, returns excess to the slab layer whenever it visits the depot, because userland has no memory pressure signal.

A per-CPU or per-thread cache is a deliberate trade of memory for scalability. Idle rounds look like a leak in heap profiles and RSS, and they multiply by the number of CPUs (or threads) and caches. Every production design pairs its caches with a sizing policy and a way to give memory back.

blocks.question: Why are full magazines only ever created as a side effect of frees, never allocated directly on the alloc path?
options: Allocating a full magazine needs M objects, which would mean M slab-layer trips, and for the magazine cache itself it would recurse forever
Full magazines are larger than empty ones
The depot lock forbids allocation
Frees are rarer than allocs
blocks.explain: Allocating empty magazines on the free path is cheap and safe. Pre-filling a magazine on the alloc path would need many objects at once, and since magazines are themselves allocated from an object cache, the first magazine allocation would need a magazine: infinite recursion. The paper notes this explicitly.

blocks.question: Over the last interval a cache's depot held between 120 and 128 full magazines. Using the paper's working-set rule, how many could be reclaimed if memory runs low?
options: 0, magazines are never reclaimed
blocks.explain: The working set is the variation, 128 minus 120 = 8 magazines. The 120 magazines that were never touched during the interval are eligible for reclaiming, just as in the paper's 37 to 47 example where 37 are reclaimable.

lessons.title: Today: thread caches, per-CPU caches and restartable sequences

blocks.md:
The magazine idea spread into user-space malloc, where there is a twist: a user program does not know which CPU it is on and cannot disable preemption. When Bonwick and Adams ported magazines to user level (libumem), they noted there was no cheap CPU ID in the thread library, and their prototype simply hashed on the thread ID. Modern allocators pick one of two answers:

- **Per-thread caches**: one cache per thread, reached through thread-local storage. No CPU ID needed and no lock on the hot path, since only that thread touches it.
- **Per-CPU caches**: one cache per logical CPU, made safe without locks or atomics by Linux **restartable sequences** (rseq).

Per-thread caches are everywhere:

- **TCMalloc** (Thread-Caching Malloc) started with per-thread caches: one singly linked free list per size class, refilled from and drained to a shared middle-end.
- **jemalloc** has a *tcache* per thread, enabled by default, caching size classes up to `opt.tcache_max` (32 KiB by default per its manual). Its manual states the trade plainly: no synchronization for most allocations, at the cost of increased memory use.
- **glibc malloc** has a per-thread *tcache*: an array of small bins, each a singly linked list capped at a small count (tunable as `glibc.malloc.tcache_count`).

TCMalloc's documentation explains why it moved on: per-thread caches give a memory footprint that scales with the number of threads, and modern programs can have thousands of threads. You either hold a lot of memory in aggregate or give each thread a minuscule cache. In per-CPU mode the number of caches is bounded by the number of logical CPUs, however many threads exist.

blocks.title: How many caches hold idle memory (simplified)

scenes.caption: Simplified model: every cache may fill to the same cap (256 KiB). Per-thread caches grow with thread count; per-CPU caches stop growing at 64 CPUs (16 MiB). Real allocators also cap the total, which instead shrinks each thread's cache.
On a 192-CPU host the per-CPU bound is 192 x 256 KiB = 48 MiB. TCMalloc's docs warn of exactly this: a slab per CPU (typically 256 KiB) means a multi-MiB footprint on big machines.

blocks.md: TCMalloc's per-CPU cache is a magazine in spirit. Each CPU has a slab of memory with a header per size class (a `current` and an `end` offset) and an array of object pointers. Allocation reads the pointer at `current - 1` and decrements `current`; free stores at `current` and increments it. Underflow refills a *batch* of objects from the middle-end, and overflow returns a batch, like a depot trade. The middle-end's **transfer cache** (one per size class, behind a mutex) is an array of pointers whose stated purpose is to let memory flow quickly from a CPU that frees to a CPU that allocates, which is the depot's job.

The hard part is safety without a lock. A thread can be preempted mid-pop and another thread can run on the same CPU and pop too. With **rseq**, the thread registers a small descriptor naming a code range `[start, commit)` and an abort address. If the kernel preempts, migrates or signals the thread while its instruction pointer is inside that range, it resumes the thread at the abort handler, which jumps back to the start. The rule that makes this work: everything before the end must be safe to redo, and the sequence ends in a single store that commits it.

blocks.prompt: Thread A on CPU 2 reads `current = 5` and loads the pointer in slot 4. Before its committing store, it is preempted and thread B runs on CPU 2 and pops slot 4. What goes wrong if A simply continues where it stopped, and what does rseq do instead?
blocks.reveal: If A continued, it would return the slot-4 object that B already returned (a double allocation) and store `current = 4`, a stale value. With rseq the kernel sees A's instruction pointer inside `[start, commit)` and resumes A at its abort handler. A restarts from the top, rereads `current = 4`, pops slot 3 and commits `current = 3`. No lock or atomic instruction was needed, because only threads on CPU 2 ever touch CPU 2's slab and the kernel serializes them.

scenes.caption: Thread A enters the pop sequence on CPU 2 and reads the header: current = 5, so the top object is in slot 4.
Before A's single committing store, the kernel preempts it and schedules thread B on the same CPU.
B performs a full pop: it returns slot 4's object and commits current = 4.
When A runs again the kernel sees its instruction pointer was inside the sequence and resumes it at the abort handler, which restarts from the top.
A rereads current = 4, takes slot 3 and commits current = 3 with one store. Both threads got distinct objects.

blocks.md: Per-thread caches need no CPU ID and work on any OS, but cost memory per thread and strand objects in threads that sleep or block (TCMalloc does return a thread's cache to the middle-end when the thread exits). Per-CPU caches bound the number of caches by CPU count but need kernel support (rseq) and careful assembly. Both keep a magazine-like batch exchange with shared state behind them.

Every modern malloc fast path is the same idea as the 2001 magazine layer: a small, private stack of free objects per thread or CPU, refilled and drained in batches from a locked shared layer, with sizing policies to cap the memory that sits idle.

blocks.question: An application runs 4,000 threads on a 32-CPU machine, most of them blocked most of the time. Which allocator front-end is the better fit for memory footprint, and why?
options: Per-thread caches, because blocked threads release their caches automatically
Per-CPU caches, because the number of caches is bounded by the 32 CPUs rather than the 4,000 threads
Neither: a global lock is best when threads are mostly blocked
Per-thread caches, because rseq does not work with more threads than CPUs
blocks.explain: Per-thread caches keep idle objects in every thread's cache, including the thousands of sleeping ones, or must shrink each cache until it is useless. Per-CPU caches exist only per logical CPU, so at most 32 hold memory, and the running threads share them.

blocks.question: In TCMalloc's rseq push (free), the code writes the object pointer into the slot and then stores the incremented `current`. Why is it fine if the thread is preempted between those two stores?
options: Preemption is disabled during free
The slot write is atomic
Nothing is published until the store to current commits; a restarted sequence just overwrites the same slot
The kernel replays the first store for it
blocks.explain: Only the final store to `current` makes the new object visible. If the thread is interrupted after writing the slot but before committing, the sequence restarts, recomputes the slot from the current header and rewrites it. TCMalloc's rseq notes describe exactly this: preempted sequences overwrite the deallocated object until one commits.
